Proof of Theorem 2

Combining Proposition 10.14 with the previously established convergence of the prefill occupancies xi​(t)→xi⋆x_{i}(t)\to x_{i}^{\star} and the fixed decode capacities in Lemma 10.7, we conclude that the fluid occupancies converge to the LP-optimal point (xi⋆,ym,i⋆,ys,i⋆)i∈[I](x_{i}^{\star},y_{m,i}^{\star},y_{s,i}^{\star})_{i\in[I]}, and the corresponding per-GPU reward attains the LP optimum. This is the key ingredient in the proof of Theorem 2 (asymptotic optimality of the gate-and-route policy).

11 Proof of the Optimality of the Prioritize-and-Route Policy

11.1 Proof of Theorem 4.2

Proof 11.1

Proof Let π~n,⋆\tilde{\pi}^{n,\star} be the prioritize-and-route policy defined in Section 4.2, parameterized by an optimal solution of the steady-state fluid LP (42).

Under separate charging, the steady-state objective (42) by which the reward only depends on aggregate occupancies (∑ixi,∑iym,i,∑iys,i)(\sum_{i}x_{i},\sum_{i}y_{m,i},\sum_{i}y_{s,i}). What is left is to prove that the prioritize-and-route policy reaches the maximal workload of the system.

The prioritize-and-route policy is work-conserving at the prefill side, so the prefill occupancy is always full. The priority index ϕi=Di/Pi\phi_{i}=D_{i}/P_{i} is proportional to the decode-work generation rate per unit prefill occupancy, since

μp,iμm,i=C/(τ​Pi)1/(τ​Di)=C​DiPi=C​ϕi.\frac{\mu_{p,i}}{\mu_{m,i}}\;=\;\frac{C/(\tau P_{i})}{1/(\tau D_{i})}\;=\;C\,\frac{D_{i}}{P_{i}}\;=\;C\,\phi_{i}.

Therefore, among all feasible ways to allocate a given amount of prefill occupancy across classes, the static priority rule maximizes the instantaneous inflow of downstream decode workload. This ensures that the aggregate decode occupancies are maximized whenever sufficient workload is available; if workload is insufficient, no policy can keep more decode capacity busy.

Consequently, the limiting fluid reward under the prioritize-and-route policy achieves the optimal value R~⋆\tilde{R}^{\star} of the steady-state LP (42), which yields the asymptotic optimality of the policy, i.e.

lim infT→∞lim infn→∞R~n​(T,π~n,⋆)=R~⋆.\liminf_{T\to\infty}\;\liminf_{n\to\infty}\;\tilde{R}_{n}(T;\tilde{\pi}^{n,\star})\;=\;\tilde{R}^{\star}.

which is exactly Theorem 4.2.

12 Proofs of the Optimality of the SLI-Aware Policy

In this section, we prove the optimality of the SLI-aware policy. Since the SLI-aware policy deals with the prefill stage the same as the Gate-and-Route policy, we will only prove the optimality of the SLI-aware policy for the decode stage. The optimality of the prefill stage follows from the optimality of the Gate-and-Route policy.

12.1 Convergence of the decode occupancies under the SLI-aware policy

In this subsection, we focus on the convergence of the decode occupancies under the SLI-aware policy.

Proposition 12.1

Fix an optimal solution (xi⋆,ym,i⋆,ys,i⋆,qp,i⋆,qd,i⋆)i∈ℐ(x_{i}^{\star},y_{m,i}^{\star},y_{s,i}^{\star},q_{p,i}^{\star},q_{d,i}^{\star})_{i\in\mathcal{I}} of the SLI-aware steady-state program (49) with qd,i⋆=0q_{d,i}^{\star}=0 for all ii. Let x⋆:=∑i=1Ixi⋆x^{\star}:=\sum_{i=1}^{I}x_{i}^{\star} and consider the corresponding static planning of the system. Denote qd,m,i​(t)q_{d,m,i}(t) and qd,s,i​(t)q_{d,s,i}(t) for the mixed and solo decode buffers under the virtual buffer split of Section 5.1 respectively. Then along any fluid trajectory of the SLI-aware policy,

limt→∞ym,i​(t)=ym,i⋆,limt→∞ys,i​(t)=ys,i⋆,limt→∞qd,s,i​(t)=0,limt→∞qd,m,i​(t)=0,∀i∈ℐ.\lim_{t\to\infty}y_{m,i}(t)=y_{m,i}^{\star},\qquad\lim_{t\to\infty}y_{s,i}(t)=y_{s,i}^{\star},\qquad\lim_{t\to\infty}q_{d,s,i}(t)=0,\qquad\lim_{t\to\infty}q_{d,m,i}(t)=0,\qquad\qquad\forall i\in\mathcal{I}.
Proof 12.2

Proof Denote the total mixed and solo decode capacities as

Cm:=x⋆​(B−1),Cs:=(1−x⋆)​B.C_{m}:=x^{\star}(B-1),\qquad C_{s}:=(1-x^{\star})B.

First we show that the decode buffer converges to zero as t→∞t\to\infty. Define the weighted decode work respectively:

Wm​(t):=∑i=1Iqd,m,i​(t)+ym,i​(t)μm,i,Ws​(t):=∑i=1Iqd,s,i​(t)+ys,i​(t)μs,i.W_{m}(t):=\sum_{i=1}^{I}\frac{q_{d,m,i}(t)+y_{m,i}(t)}{\mu_{m,i}},\qquad W_{s}(t):=\sum_{i=1}^{I}\frac{q_{d,s,i}(t)+y_{s,i}(t)}{\mu_{s,i}}.

Take the derivative of the formulas above, we have:

W˙m​(t)\displaystyle\dot{W}_{m}(t) =∑i=1I(1−ps,i)​μp,iμm,i​xi​(t)−ym​(t)−∑i=1Iθiμm,i​qd,m,i​(t),\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{I}\frac{(1-p_{s,i})\,\mu_{p,i}}{\mu_{m,i}}\,x_{i}(t)\;-\;y_{m}(t)\;-\;\sum_{i=1}^{I}\frac{\theta_{i}}{\mu_{m,i}}\,q_{d,m,i}(t), (63)
W˙s​(t)\displaystyle\dot{W}_{s}(t) =∑i=1Ips,i​μp,iμs,i​xi​(t)−ys​(t)−∑i=1Iθiμs,i​qd,s,i​(t).\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{I}\frac{p_{s,i}\,\mu_{p,i}}{\mu_{s,i}}\,x_{i}(t)\;-\;y_{s}(t)\;-\;\sum_{i=1}^{I}\frac{\theta_{i}}{\mu_{s,i}}\,q_{d,s,i}(t). (64)

Here ym​(t):=∑iym,i​(t)y_{m}(t):=\sum_{i}y_{m,i}(t) and ys​(t):=∑iys,i​(t)y_{s}(t):=\sum_{i}y_{s,i}(t).

Whenever qd,m​(t)>0q_{d,m}(t)>0, the mixed group is work-conserving, so all mixed decode slots are busy and ym​(t)=Cmy_{m}(t)=C_{m}; similarly, qd,s​(t)>0q_{d,s}(t)>0 implies ys​(t)=Csy_{s}(t)=C_{s}. Since xi​(t)→xi⋆x_{i}(t)\to x_{i}^{\star} and the LP feasibility constraints include ∑iym,i⋆≤Cm\sum_{i}y_{m,i}^{\star}\leq C_{m} and ∑iys,i⋆≤Cs\sum_{i}y_{s,i}^{\star}\leq C_{s}, the constants

Am⋆:=∑i=1I(1−ps,i)​μp,iμm,i​xi⋆,As⋆:=∑i=1Ips,i​μp,iμs,i​xi⋆A_{m}^{\star}:=\sum_{i=1}^{I}\frac{(1-p_{s,i})\,\mu_{p,i}}{\mu_{m,i}}\,x_{i}^{\star},\qquad A_{s}^{\star}:=\sum_{i=1}^{I}\frac{p_{s,i}\,\mu_{p,i}}{\mu_{s,i}}\,x_{i}^{\star}

satisfy Am⋆≤CmA_{m}^{\star}\leq C_{m} and As⋆≤CsA_{s}^{\star}\leq C_{s}, since they are both the admission limit of the policy which should be less than the total decode capacity. Therefore,

qd,m​(t)>0⟹W˙m​(t)≤−θ¯m​qd,m​(t),qd,s​(t)>0⟹W˙s​(t)≤−θ¯s​qd,s​(t),q_{d,m}(t)>0\ \Longrightarrow\ \dot{W}_{m}(t)\leq-\underline{\theta}_{m}\,q_{d,m}(t),\qquad q_{d,s}(t)>0\ \Longrightarrow\ \dot{W}_{s}(t)\leq-\underline{\theta}_{s}\,q_{d,s}(t),

where θ¯m:=mini⁡θi/μm,i>0\underline{\theta}_{m}:=\min_{i}\theta_{i}/\mu_{m,i}>0 and θ¯s:=mini⁡θi/μs,i>0\underline{\theta}_{s}:=\min_{i}\theta_{i}/\mu_{s,i}>0. The same contradiction argument as in Proposition 10.14 implies

limt→∞qd,m​(t)=0,limt→∞qd,s​(t)=0.\lim_{t\to\infty}q_{d,m}(t)=0,\qquad\lim_{t\to\infty}q_{d,s}(t)=0.

Now we are ready to show the convergence of the decode occupancies respectively. By our policy, we can compute the instant admission rates of the mixed and solo decode pools respectively:

u˙d,m,i​(t)=(1−ps,i)​(μp,i​xi​(t)−θi​qd,s,i​(t)),u˙d,s,i​(t)=ps,i​(μp,i​xi​(t)−θi​qd,m,i​(t))\dot{u}_{d,m,i}(t)=(1-p_{s,i})\,(\mu_{p,i}\,x_{i}(t)-\theta_{i}q_{d,s,i}(t)),\qquad\dot{u}_{d,s,i}(t)=p_{s,i}\,(\mu_{p,i}\,x_{i}(t)-\theta_{i}q_{d,m,i}(t))

Take the derivative of the decode occupancies of the balance equations, we have:

y˙m,i​(t)=(1−ps,i)​μp,i​xi​(t)−μm,i​ym,i​(t),y˙s,i​(t)=ps,i​μp,i​xi​(t)−μs,i​ys,i​(t),\dot{y}_{m,i}(t)=(1-p_{s,i})\,\mu_{p,i}\,x_{i}(t)-\mu_{m,i}\,y_{m,i}(t),\qquad\dot{y}_{s,i}(t)=p_{s,i}\,\mu_{p,i}\,x_{i}(t)-\mu_{s,i}\,y_{s,i}(t),

Since xi​(t)→xi⋆x_{i}(t)\to x_{i}^{\star} and qd,m,i​(t)→0q_{d,m,i}(t)\to 0 and qd,s,i​(t)→0q_{d,s,i}(t)\to 0 and the LP feasibility condition:

μp,i​xi⋆=μm,i​ym,i⋆+μs,i​ys,i⋆\mu_{p,i}x_{i}^{\star}=\mu_{m,i}y_{m,i}^{\star}+\mu_{s,i}y_{s,i}^{\star}

then for any ϵ>0\epsilon>0, there exists TϵT_{\epsilon} such that for all t≥Tϵt\geq T_{\epsilon},

|μ˙d,s,i​(t)−μs,i​ys,i⋆|≤ϵ\displaystyle|\dot{\mu}_{d,s,i}(t)-\mu_{s,i}y_{s,i}^{\star}|\leq\epsilon
|μ˙d,m,i​(t)−μm,i​ym,i⋆|≤ϵ\displaystyle|\dot{\mu}_{d,m,i}(t)-\mu_{m,i}y_{m,i}^{\star}|\leq\epsilon

Then we have:

μm,i​ym,i∗−ϵ≤y˙s,i​(t)+μm,i​ym,i​(t)≤μm,i​ym,i∗+ϵ\displaystyle\mu_{m,i}y_{m,i}^{*}-\epsilon\leq\dot{y}_{s,i}(t)+\mu_{m,i}y_{m,i}(t)\leq\mu_{m,i}y_{m,i}^{*}+\epsilon
μs,i​ys,i∗−ϵ≤y˙s,i​(t)+μs,i​ys,i​(t)≤μs,i​ys,i∗+ϵ\displaystyle\mu_{s,i}y_{s,i}^{*}-\epsilon\leq\dot{y}_{s,i}(t)+\mu_{s,i}y_{s,i}(t)\leq\mu_{s,i}y_{s,i}^{*}+\epsilon

Solving the above inequalities and let ϵ→0\epsilon\to 0 and t→∞t\to\infty, we have:

limt→∞ym,i​(t)=ym,i⋆,limt→∞ys,i​(t)=ys,i⋆,∀i∈ℐ.\lim_{t\to\infty}y_{m,i}(t)=y_{m,i}^{\star},\qquad\lim_{t\to\infty}y_{s,i}(t)=y_{s,i}^{\star},\qquad\forall i\in\mathcal{I}.

which means that the decode occupancies converge to the LP targets.

13 General SLI-aware Policy

In this section, we analyze the general SLI-aware setting under mild regularity on the optimization problem (bounded penalties, etc.), in which case the SLI-aware LP may admit an optimal solution with qd,i⋆>0q_{d,i}^{\star}>0 for some ii.

General SLI-aware Policy

Fix an optimal solution of the SLI-aware LP (xi⋆,ym,i⋆,ys,i⋆,qp,i⋆,qd,i⋆)i∈ℐ(x_{i}^{\star},y_{m,i}^{\star},y_{s,i}^{\star},q_{p,i}^{\star},q_{d,i}^{\star})_{i\in\mathcal{I}}, allowing qd,i⋆>0q_{d,i}^{\star}>0. As in Section 5.1, we partition GPUs into Gmix(n)G_{\mathrm{mix}}^{(n)} and Gsolo(n)G_{\mathrm{solo}}^{(n)} according to the static planning. We split the decode buffer into mixed buffer and solo buffer and track the queue lengths Qd,m,in​(t)Q_{d,m,i}^{n}(t) and Qd,s,in​(t)Q_{d,s,i}^{n}(t) accordingly. Upon each class-ii prefill completion, we route the resulting decode job to the solo buffer with probability ps,ip_{s,i} and to the mixed buffer with probability 1−ps,i1-p_{s,i}.

We set the pool-selection probabilities

ps,i:={μs,i​ys,i⋆μm,i​ym,i⋆+μs,i​ys,i⋆,if ​μm,i​ym,i⋆+μs,i​ys,i⋆>0,1,otherwise.p_{s,i}\;:=\;\begin{cases}\dfrac{\mu_{s,i}\,y_{s,i}^{\star}}{\mu_{m,i}\,y_{m,i}^{\star}+\mu_{s,i}\,y_{s,i}^{\star}},&\text{if }\mu_{m,i}y_{m,i}^{\star}+\mu_{s,i}y_{s,i}^{\star}>0,\\[8.0pt] 1,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

When qd,i⋆>0q_{d,i}^{\star}>0, the LP flow-balance implies

μm,i​ym,i⋆+μs,i​ys,i⋆=μp,i​xi⋆−θi​qd,i⋆,\mu_{m,i}y_{m,i}^{\star}+\mu_{s,i}y_{s,i}^{\star}\;=\;\mu_{p,i}x_{i}^{\star}-\theta_{i}q_{d,i}^{\star},

so the definition of ps,ip_{s,i} above can be rewritten as

ps,i=μs,i​ys,i⋆μp,i​xi⋆−θi​qd,i⋆,p_{s,i}\;=\;\frac{\mu_{s,i}y_{s,i}^{\star}}{\mu_{p,i}x_{i}^{\star}-\theta_{i}q_{d,i}^{\star}},

i.e., ps,ip_{s,i} is the solo share of the net decode completion rate. Accordingly, we have the consistent pool-level queue split

qd,s,i⋆:=ps,i​qd,i⋆,qd,m,i⋆:=(1−ps,i)​qd,i⋆.q_{d,s,i}^{\star}:=p_{s,i}\,q_{d,i}^{\star},\qquad q_{d,m,i}^{\star}:=(1-p_{s,i})\,q_{d,i}^{\star}.

We additionally define pool class selection weights (with the convention 0/0:=00/0:=0)

ϖm,i:=μm,i​ym,i⋆∑j∈ℐμm,j​ym,j⋆,ϖs,i:=μs,i​ys,i⋆∑j∈ℐμs,j​ys,j⋆.\varpi_{m,i}\;:=\;\frac{\mu_{m,i}y_{m,i}^{\star}}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}}\mu_{m,j}y_{m,j}^{\star}},\qquad\varpi_{s,i}\;:=\;\frac{\mu_{s,i}y_{s,i}^{\star}}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}}\mu_{s,j}y_{s,j}^{\star}}.

Different from the baseline SLI-aware policy, in the general SLI-aware policy, we introduce a pool class selection rule within each pool.

(i) Solo-pool class selection. Whenever a solo decode slot becomes available and ∑iQd,s,in​(t−)>0\sum_{i}Q_{d,s,i}^{n}(t^{-})>0, the decode scheduler selects a class according to the weights {ϖs,i}i∈ℐ\{\varpi_{s,i}\}_{i\in\mathcal{I}} restricted to currently nonempty solo decode buffer:

ℙ⁡(select class ​i|{Qd,s,jn​(t−)}j)=ϖs,i 1{Qd,s,in(t−)>0}∑j∈ℐϖs,j 1{Qd,s,jn(t−)>0}.\mathbb{P}\!\left(\text{select class }i\,\middle|\,\{Q_{d,s,j}^{n}(t^{-})\}_{j}\right)\;=\;\frac{\varpi_{s,i}\,\mathbf{1}\{Q_{d,s,i}^{n}(t^{-})>0\}}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}}\varpi_{s,j}\,\mathbf{1}\{Q_{d,s,j}^{n}(t^{-})>0\}}.

It then routes the head-of-line job of that class to the freed solo slot. If the solo decode buffer is empty, the slot idles.

(ii) Mixed-pool class selection. Whenever a mixed decode slot becomes available and ∑iQd,m,in​(t−)>0\sum_{i}Q_{d,m,i}^{n}(t^{-})>0, the scheduler selects a class according to {ϖm,i}\{\varpi_{m,i}\} restricted to nonempty mixed decode buffer (defined analogously) and routes the corresponding head-of-line job to the freed mixed slot.

This policy is work-conserving within each pool and preserves FCFS within each class buffer. It differs from the baseline SLI-aware router only in the cross-class selection rule within the mixed/solo decode pools. Then we focus on the fluid dynamics induced by the general SLI-aware policy. We focus on the case where the SLI-aware LP solution satisfies qd,i⋆>0q_{d,i}^{\star}>0 for all ii and both decode capacity constraints bind. The proof for boundary cases (some qd,i⋆=0q_{d,i}^{\star}=0, etc.) is analogous.

First, we introduce some conventions for the general SLI-aware policy. Let qd,m,i​(t)q_{d,m,i}(t) and qd,s,i​(t)q_{d,s,i}(t) denote the mixed/solo decode queue contents, and ud,m,i​(t)u_{d,m,i}(t) and ud,s,i​(t)u_{d,s,i}(t) denote the cumulative admissions into mixed/solo decode service. Abandonments occur from each pool buffer at rate θi\theta_{i}, i.e.,

b˙d,m,i​(t)=θi​qd,m,i​(t),b˙d,s,i​(t)=θi​qd,s,i​(t),\dot{b}_{d,m,i}(t)=\theta_{i}q_{d,m,i}(t),\qquad\dot{b}_{d,s,i}(t)=\theta_{i}q_{d,s,i}(t),

and the total queue length is qd,i​(t)=qd,m,i​(t)+qd,s,i​(t)q_{d,i}(t)=q_{d,m,i}(t)+q_{d,s,i}(t).

Lemma 13.1

Fix a regular time tt at which all fluid coordinates are differentiable. Define the aggregate decode admission and completion rates

u˙d,m​(t):=∑i∈ℐu˙d,m,i​(t),u˙d,s​(t):=∑i∈ℐu˙d,s,i​(t),d˙d,m​(t):=∑i∈ℐμm,i​ym,i​(t),d˙d,s​(t):=∑i∈ℐμs,i​ys,i​(t).\dot{u}_{d,m}(t):=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\dot{u}_{d,m,i}(t),\quad\dot{u}_{d,s}(t):=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\dot{u}_{d,s,i}(t),\quad\dot{d}_{d,m}(t):=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\mu_{m,i}y_{m,i}(t),\quad\dot{d}_{d,s}(t):=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\mu_{s,i}y_{s,i}(t).

If the corresponding pool buffer is positive at time tt, then that pool is work-conserving:

qd,m​(t)>0⟹u˙d,m​(t)=d˙d,m​(t),qd,s​(t)>0⟹u˙d,s​(t)=d˙d,s​(t).q_{d,m}(t)>0\ \Longrightarrow\ \dot{u}_{d,m}(t)=\dot{d}_{d,m}(t),\qquad q_{d,s}(t)>0\ \Longrightarrow\ \dot{u}_{d,s}(t)=\dot{d}_{d,s}(t).

Moreover, under the within-pool class selection rule,

qd,m​(t)>0\displaystyle q_{d,m}(t)>0 ⟹u˙d,m,i​(t)=u˙d,m​(t)​ϖm,i 1{qd,m,i(t)>0}∑j∈ℐϖm,j 1{qd,m,j(t)>0},\displaystyle\Longrightarrow\ \dot{u}_{d,m,i}(t)=\dot{u}_{d,m}(t)\,\frac{\varpi_{m,i}\,\mathbf{1}\{q_{d,m,i}(t)>0\}}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}}\varpi_{m,j}\,\mathbf{1}\{q_{d,m,j}(t)>0\}},
qd,s​(t)>0\displaystyle q_{d,s}(t)>0 ⟹u˙d,s,i​(t)=u˙d,s​(t)​ϖs,i 1{qd,s,i(t)>0}∑j∈ℐϖs,j 1{qd,s,j(t)>0}.\displaystyle\Longrightarrow\ \dot{u}_{d,s,i}(t)=\dot{u}_{d,s}(t)\,\frac{\varpi_{s,i}\,\mathbf{1}\{q_{d,s,i}(t)>0\}}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}}\varpi_{s,j}\,\mathbf{1}\{q_{d,s,j}(t)>0\}}.
Proof 13.2

Proof If qd,∙​(t)>0q_{d,\bullet}(t)>0 for ∙∈{m,s}\bullet\in\{m,s\}, then the corresponding pool buffer is nonempty and the policy is work-conserving on that pool: If a decode slot is free, then a job will be routed to the slot immediately. Hence u˙d,∙​(t)=d˙d,∙​(t)\dot{u}_{d,\bullet}(t)=\dot{d}_{d,\bullet}(t). The instant admission formulas follow directly from the definition of pool selection rule: at the fluid scale, each pool’s admissions inherit the fixed weights ϖ∙,i\varpi_{\bullet,i} restricted to nonempty class buffers.

Lemma 13.3

Fix μ∈ℝ+⁣+I\mu\in\mathbb{R}^{I}_{++} and v∈ℝ+⁣+Iv\in\mathbb{R}^{I}_{++} with ∑i=1Ivi=1\sum_{i=1}^{I}v_{i}=1. Let D:=diag⁡(μ1,…,μI)D:=\mathrm{diag}(\mu_{1},\ldots,\mu_{I}) and A:=v​μ⊤−DA:=v\mu^{\top}-D. Then:

  1. (i)

    00 is a simple eigenvalue of AA and all other eigenvalues have strictly negative real parts.

  2. (ii)

    For the ODE y˙​(t)=A​y​(t)\dot{y}(t)=Ay(t), 𝟏⊤​y​(t)\mathbf{1}^{\top}y(t) is conserved and

    y⁡(t)⟶y∞:=(𝟏⊤​y​(0))​D−1​v𝟏⊤​D−1​vas ​t→∞.y(t)\ \longrightarrow\ y^{\infty}:=\bigl(\mathbf{1}^{\top}y(0)\bigr)\,\frac{D^{-1}v}{\mathbf{1}^{\top}D^{-1}v}\qquad\text{as }t\to\infty.
Proof 13.4

Proof (i):By the matrix determinant lemma,

det(λ​I−A)=det(λ​I+D−v​μ⊤)=det(λ​I+D)​(1−μ⊤​(λ​I+D)−1​v).\det(\lambda I-A)=\det(\lambda I+D-v\mu^{\top})=\det(\lambda I+D)\Bigl(1-\mu^{\top}(\lambda I+D)^{-1}v\Bigr).

Hence λ\lambda is an eigenvalue of AA if and only if

At λ=0\lambda=0, the right-hand side equals ∑ivi=1\sum_{i}v_{i}=1, so λ=0\lambda=0 is an eigenvalue. Its simplicity follows because the derivative of the right-hand side at λ=0\lambda=0 equals −∑ivi/μi≠0-\sum_{i}v_{i}/\mu_{i}\neq 0. Next, let λ\lambda satisfy Re⁡(λ)≥0\mathrm{Re}(\lambda)\geq 0 and λ≠0\lambda\neq 0. Then for each ii,

|μiλ+μi|<μiRe⁡(λ)+μi≤1,\left|\frac{\mu_{i}}{\lambda+\mu_{i}}\right|<\frac{\mu_{i}}{\mathrm{Re}(\lambda)+\mu_{i}}\leq 1,

with strict inequality because λ≠0\lambda\neq 0. Therefore

|∑i=1Ivi​μiλ+μi|≤∑i=1Ivi​|μiλ+μi|<∑i=1Ivi=1,\left|\sum_{i=1}^{I}v_{i}\,\frac{\mu_{i}}{\lambda+\mu_{i}}\right|\leq\sum_{i=1}^{I}v_{i}\left|\frac{\mu_{i}}{\lambda+\mu_{i}}\right|<\sum_{i=1}^{I}v_{i}=1,

so the eigenvalue equation cannot hold. This shows that 00 is the only eigenvalue with nonnegative real part.

(ii): Since A=v​μ⊤−DA=v\mu^{\top}-D and ∑ivi=1\sum_{i}v_{i}=1, we have

𝟏⊤​A=𝟏⊤​(v​μ⊤)−𝟏⊤​D=(𝟏⊤​v)​μ⊤−μ⊤=𝟎⊤.\mathbf{1}^{\top}A=\mathbf{1}^{\top}(v\mu^{\top})-\mathbf{1}^{\top}D=(\mathbf{1}^{\top}v)\mu^{\top}-\mu^{\top}=\mathbf{0}^{\top}.

Therefore, along any absolutely continuous solution of y˙​(t)=A​y​(t)\dot{y}(t)=Ay(t),

dd​t​ 1⊤​y​(t)=𝟏⊤​y˙​(t)=𝟏⊤​A​y​(t)=0\frac{d}{dt}\,\mathbf{1}^{\top}y(t)=\mathbf{1}^{\top}\dot{y}(t)=\mathbf{1}^{\top}Ay(t)=0

so the total mass M:=𝟏⊤​y​(t)M:=\mathbf{1}^{\top}y(t) is conserved: M=𝟏⊤​y​(0)M=\mathbf{1}^{\top}y(0) for all tt. The equilibrium set is the kernel of AA. If A​y=0Ay=0, then

0=Ay=v(μ⊤y)−Dy⟺Dy=(μ⊤y)v.0=Ay=v(\mu^{\top}y)-Dy\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad Dy=(\mu^{\top}y)\,v.

y=s​D−1​v.y=s\,D^{-1}v.

M=𝟏⊤​y=s​ 1⊤​D−1​v⟹s=M𝟏⊤​D−1​v.M=\mathbf{1}^{\top}y=s\,\mathbf{1}^{\top}D^{-1}v\quad\Longrightarrow\quad s=\frac{M}{\mathbf{1}^{\top}D^{-1}v}.

By part (i), all eigenvalues of AA other than 00 have strictly negative real parts, and 00 is a simple eigenvalue. P:=r​ 1⊤𝟏⊤​r=D−1​v​ 1⊤𝟏⊤​D−1​v.P:=\frac{r\,\mathbf{1}^{\top}}{\mathbf{1}^{\top}r}=\frac{D^{-1}v\,\mathbf{1}^{\top}}{\mathbf{1}^{\top}D^{-1}v}.

Proposition 13.5

Assume θi>0\theta_{i}>0 for all i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I}. Under the refined SLI-aware policy above, every fluid solution satisfies

limt→∞xi​(t)=xi⋆,limt→∞ym,i​(t)=ym,i⋆,limt→∞ys,i​(t)=ys,i⋆,limt→∞qd,i​(t)=qd,i⋆,\lim_{t\to\infty}x_{i}(t)=x_{i}^{\star},\qquad\lim_{t\to\infty}y_{m,i}(t)=y_{m,i}^{\star},\qquad\lim_{t\to\infty}y_{s,i}(t)=y_{s,i}^{\star},\qquad\lim_{t\to\infty}q_{d,i}(t)=q_{d,i}^{\star},

for all i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I}.

Proof 13.6

Proof The prefill part mainly follows from the proof of Theorem 4.1. Therefore the prefill argument in the proof of Theorem 4.1 applies verbatim, and there exists Tp<∞T_{p}<\infty such that for all t≥Tpt\geq T_{p} and all i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I},

qp,i​(t)>0,xi​(t)=xi⋆.q_{p,i}(t)>0,\qquad x_{i}(t)=x_{i}^{\star}. (65)

We analyze the decode dynamics on [Tp,∞)[T_{p},\infty) and shift the time origin so that (65) holds for all t≥0t\geq 0.

Then the resulting constant pool arrival rates are

αs,i:=ps,i​μp,i​xi⋆,αm,i:=(1−ps,i)​μp,i​xi⋆,i∈ℐ,\alpha_{s,i}:=p_{s,i}\mu_{p,i}x_{i}^{\star},\qquad\alpha_{m,i}:=(1-p_{s,i})\mu_{p,i}x_{i}^{\star},\qquad i\in\mathcal{I},

and the pool capacities

ys⋆:=∑i∈ℐys,i⋆,ym⋆:=∑i∈ℐym,i⋆,y_{s}^{\star}:=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}y_{s,i}^{\star},\qquad y_{m}^{\star}:=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}y_{m,i}^{\star},

which coincide with the binding decode capacity constraints at the LP optimum.

The differential version of the balance equations give:

together with the corresponding in-service dynamics y˙s,i​(t)=u˙d,s,i​(t)−μs,i​ys,i​(t)\dot{y}_{s,i}(t)=\dot{u}_{d,s,i}(t)-\mu_{s,i}y_{s,i}(t) and y˙m,i​(t)=u˙d,m,i​(t)−μm,i​ym,i​(t)\dot{y}_{m,i}(t)=\dot{u}_{d,m,i}(t)-\mu_{m,i}y_{m,i}(t) under the static planning.

Since both pools are work-conserving for all t≥T0t\geq T_{0}. Therefore the admission rates satisfy

qd,s,i​(t)=e−θi​(t−T0)​qd,s,i​(T0)+∫T0te−θi​(t−u)​(αs,i−ϖs,i​∑j∈ℐμs,j​ys,j​(u))​𝑑u.q_{d,s,i}(t)=e^{-\theta_{i}(t-T_{0})}\,q_{d,s,i}(T_{0})\;+\;\int_{T_{0}}^{t}e^{-\theta_{i}(t-u)}\Bigl(\alpha_{s,i}-\varpi_{s,i}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}}\mu_{s,j}y_{s,j}(u)\Bigr)\,du.

Since ys,i​(u)→ys,i⋆y_{s,i}(u)\to y_{s,i}^{\star} for each ii, the integrand converges to αs,i−ϖs,i​∑j∈ℐμs,j​ys,j⋆=αs,i−μs,i​ys,i⋆=θi​qd,s,i⋆\alpha_{s,i}-\varpi_{s,i}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{I}}\mu_{s,j}y_{s,j}^{\star}=\alpha_{s,i}-\mu_{s,i}y_{s,i}^{\star}=\theta_{i}q_{d,s,i}^{\star}. Standard arguments for linear convolution with an exponentially decaying kernel (or directly applying dominated convergence) then yield qd,s,i​(t)→qd,s,i⋆q_{d,s,i}(t)\to q_{d,s,i}^{\star} as t→∞t\to\infty. The same argument applied to the mixed pool queue gives qd,m,i​(t)→qd,m,i⋆q_{d,m,i}(t)\to q_{d,m,i}^{\star}. Summing gives qd,i​(t)=qd,m,i​(t)+qd,s,i​(t)→qd,i⋆q_{d,i}(t)=q_{d,m,i}(t)+q_{d,s,i}(t)\to q_{d,i}^{\star}.

14 Additional Experiments and Empirical Validation

This section provides additional empirical validations that complement the main text. We first provide a comprehensive analysis of workload heterogeneity through task-level statistics and visualization in the (P,D)(P,D) space. We then validate the exponential distribution assumption for output lengths by fitting empirical data and calculating divergence metrics. Finally, we detail the computing infrastructure used for our measurements and simulations.

Workload heterogeneity and task characteristics.

Table 1 reports the average prompt (input) and output lengths for eight task categories from the Databricks Dolly-15k instruction-tuning dataset (Conover et al., 2023). The data reveals substantial variation across categories. For example, summarization and information extraction tasks average over 1,000 input tokens with moderate output. In contrast, creative writing and open QA require fewer than 100 input tokens yet generate longer outputs on average.

To further illustrate this heterogeneity, Figure 11 plots the input and output length pairs for two representative categories: Information Extraction and Creative Writing. These two classes exhibit nearly opposite characteristics. Information Extraction tasks cluster in the high-input and low-output region. Creative Writing tasks concentrate in the low-input and high-output zone. This contrast confirms that a uniform scheduling policy cannot efficiently balance resources across diverse workloads, which motivates the multiclass framework developed in this paper.

Validation of the exponential distribution assumption.

Our model assumes exponentially distributed output lengths for each task class. This assumption directly determines the decode service rate in our stochastic network. To check whether this approximation is reasonable, we fit exponential distributions to the actual output length data from the Databricks Dolly-15k dataset using Maximum Likelihood Estimation.

Figure 12 compares the empirical CDFs with the fitted exponential CDFs for all eight task categories. The exponential fit is good for most categories. Brainstorming, Classification, Closed QA, Information Extraction, Open QA, and Summarization all track closely. General QA shows reasonable agreement despite some mid-range deviation. Creative Writing deviates more noticeably in the upper tail. This is likely because its output distribution is heavier-tailed than a pure exponential, which is consistent with its high mean and variance.

To complement the visual comparison, Table 2 reports the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between the empirical output-length distribution and its fitted exponential approximation for each category. Smaller values indicate closer agreement. Overall, the exponential assumption captures the main characteristics of the distributions well enough to justify its use for analytical tractability.
